claim: The 101>100 wall_time_ms failure is a fixture artifact, not a correctness budget. minimal-deployment-request-cell-runtime-readiness.test.js sets wall_time_ms:100 in the SHARED definition() fixture used by every test in the file including happy-path readiness, so on a contended runner an ordinary invocation trips it. Budget-exhaustion correctness in that same file is proven deterministically by input instead: the dedicated exhaustion test asserts input_bytes (via a 100-char arg) and cpu_time_ms (via args [3]), never wall clock. No test in the repo asserts 'wall_time_ms budget exhausted'. Every sibling test that actually executes a component uses a far looser wall budget (worker-modes 300000, movielens 60000, time-binding 500, once-binding 250), so 100 is an outlier. Repair is to give the wall-clock watchdog slack in the fixture, which removes the machine-speed dependency without weakening any exhaustion assertion.

Neither census test fails without contention. On b8cd88bd5, check-operation-dispatch-completion-owner passed 5/5 and impact-proof-cone-consumers passed 5/5 run serially at --jobs=1. Neither contains randomness (no Math.random, no fast-check, no seed), so their inputs are deterministic, and neither mutates the live working tree: impact-proof-cone-consumers writes only under a temp fixtureRoot (its FORGED_TEST_PATH 'test/ghost.test.js' is fixture-relative) and completion-owner performs no filesystem writes at all. Correction to an earlier reading: the apparent census diff in the CI log is NOT the assertion diff. The gate's dump step greps the artifact with '^(not ok|# test-files.*fail=[1-9]|FAIL|.*[Ee]rror)', so only diff lines whose filenames contain 'error' survived; the real diff was never in the log. Diagnosis therefore requires reproduction under concurrency, not further log reading.

'Component startup timed out' originates in PRODUCTION source, not a test fixture: src/runtime/wasi-component-cell-runtime.js:23 hardcodes STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000 (and HEALTH_TIMEOUT_MS = 1_000), enforced by waitForReady() as a wall-clock setTimeout. Under contention a legitimate wasm component startup exceeds 10s and the cell is declared START_FAILED. The CI file durations (service-cell-bridge-roundtrip 146908ms, service-cell-worker-modes 93434ms) are consistent with several startups each burning the full 10s timeout. This makes the failure a product robustness question, not only a test-harness one: the runtime treats a slow-but-healthy start as a failure with no distinction between 'slow' and 'broken'. Any repair here changes runtime behaviour and must not be done by quietly widening the constant; first establish from the jobs=1/2/4 experiment whether startup exceeds 10s only under oversubscription.

The execution model classifies tests by PATH but these tests declare their nature by FILENAME, so a whole class escapes the serial lane. test:fast excludes only 'test/integration/*' and 'test/bootstrap/*', yet 15 files are named *.integration.test.js outside test/integration/; 14 of them (all but the bootstrap one) therefore run at --jobs=4. They are also absent from every test/shards/*.txt list, so unlike their 62 siblings under test/integration/ (which run at --jobs=1 via test:integration:1..3) they NEVER run serially anywhere. One of the persistent cloud failures, test/cdc/current-epoch-propagation.integration.test.js, is exactly in this leaked set, as are postgres-wire-adapter, wasm-call-adapter, distributed-debug-e2e and replica-dispatch-atomic-claim. This is a defect in the CI execution model itself rather than in the tests: the serial contract exists and these files silently fall outside it.

The dt6/cdc 'timeout!' failures are tap's 30s per-test cap, not vague starvation, and the repo already documents this exact class. run-test-files.js:198-213 records the 2026-08-04 discovery that this tap version silently caps every test at 30s and that neither the test option nor t.setTimeout() can extend it; only the TAP_TIMEOUT env does, so the harness lifts TAP_TIMEOUT to the largest {timeout: NNNN} declared in the file (TIMEOUT_OPTION_PATTERN requires 4+ digits). Measured against the failing files: all three dt6 tests (rebalancer-timeout-detection-network, cpu-saturation-missed-budget-spike, rebalancer-timeout-orchestration-network) declare NO timeout option at all, so they run under the bare 30s cap while their cloud durations were 44413ms, 77632ms and 32996ms; cdc/current-epoch-propagation.integration declares exactly {timeout: 30000}, equal to the default and therefore zero headroom, against a 47444ms cloud duration. Declaring a realistic per-file timeout changes only the wall-clock cap the harness allows, never an assertion, so it is categorically different from widening a product budget like STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS.

The wasm/service-cell cluster fails by TWO distinct wall-clock mechanisms, and neither file declares a timeout. All five (service-cell-world-abi, service-compiler-module-shape-spike, service-compiler-editor-typings, service-cell-bridge-roundtrip, service-cell-worker-modes) declare no {timeout: NNNN}, so all run under tap's bare 30s cap. On b8cd88bd5 the cloud run split them: world-abi and module-shape-spike failed with tap 'not ok 1 - timeout!' (file totals 175569ms and 159911ms), while bridge-roundtrip and worker-modes failed with the PRODUCT error 'Component startup timed out' from STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS=10_000. Locally on a 20-core box these same files already take 31766ms (world-abi), 31785ms (worker-modes), 36049ms (bridge-roundtrip) and 27650ms (v2-world-abi) — i.e. they sit against the 30s cap at FULL speed with no margin, which is why any slowdown tips them over. The harness-cap half is a safe declaration fix; the STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS half is a product-behaviour question and stays untouched.

CORRECTION of my own earlier hypothesis: check-operation-dispatch-completion-owner is NOT shared-state interference, it is the same tap 30s cap. The tell is the tap total, not the subtest: the file reports '# time=30249.93ms' (just over the 30000ms cap) while the subtest blamed took only 10.638ms. Whichever subtest is in flight when the cap expires is the one reported failed, which fully explains the shifting identity across runs (CI run1 'missing REPLACE target-active cleanup', CI run2 'weak REPLACE target-active cleanup', local jobs=4 'a parallel delivered-create registry') without invoking a race. The file declares no {timeout: NNNN}, and its durations track load exactly: ~9.5s local jobs=1 PASS, 34909ms local jobs=4-on-2-cores FAIL, 47064ms and 45851ms on CI FAIL. Reproduced faithfully under taskset -c 0,1 at jobs=4, which also reproduced the other CI errors verbatim including 'wall_time_ms budget exhausted (101 > 100)' with identical numbers. So a shifting failure identity is NOT by itself evidence of a race when an unbounded harness cap can land anywhere in the file.

Oversubscription confirmed with a deterministic threshold, measured under taskset -c 0,1 to emulate the 2-vCPU runner. jobs=1: 2/2 reps pass (168s,166s). jobs=2: 2/2 reps pass (153s,152s). jobs=4: 2/2 reps FAIL, and the SAME four files fail both times (minimal-deployment-request-cell-runtime-readiness, service-cell-worker-modes, check-operation-dispatch-completion-owner, service-cell-bridge-roundtrip) - a reproducible contention threshold, not random flake. Per-file durations scale with contention: bridge-roundtrip 50103ms at jobs=1 -> 90877ms at jobs=2 -> 135165ms at jobs=4; completion-owner 10051ms -> 21261ms -> 34909ms. Key mechanical detail: tap's 30s cap is per-SUBTEST, not per-file, which is why files whose TOTAL is already 43-50s at jobs=1 still pass - their individual subtests stay under 30s - and only break once contention stretches a subtest past 30s. Cost/benefit is decisive: total wall clock is 168s at jobs=1, 153s at jobs=2, 135s at jobs=4, so jobs=4 buys ~20% on this corpus while destroying determinism, and jobs=2 captures most of the saving while staying green 2/2.

The alarming wizer error is a CASCADE of the 30s cap, not an independent fault. service-init-wasm-scaffold passes in isolation at jobs=1 in 17519ms, so nothing is structurally broken. Its makeTempRoot registers t.teardown(() => rm(root, {recursive:true, force:true})); when a subtest is killed by the cap, tap runs that teardown and deletes /tmp/lagrange-wasm-init-XXXX while the still-running toolchain child is mid-build, so wizer then reports 'failed to open directory: /tmp/lagrange-wasm-init-*/amounts-service ... No such file or directory'. The CI evidence fits: subtests 3 and 4 both reported the IDENTICAL time=89114.479ms, the signature of one cap expiry attributed to several subtests, with a file total of 92239ms. Second measurement, important for runner sizing: this test alone burns ~3.7 cores (real 17.5s vs user 64s), because the wasm toolchain parallelises internally. So on a 2-vCPU runner even jobs=2 can oversubscribe when both slots hold toolchain tests, and a naive per-file job count understates true CPU demand. Prediction to verify after the lane repair: the wizer ENOENT disappears with no change to wizer or the scaffold.

CORRECTION of my own earlier claim that no test asserts wall_time_ms exhaustion: one does, and it is already deterministic in exactly the prescribed way. minimal-deployment-request-cell-runtime-readiness.test.js:547-566 builds definitionWithBudgets({cpu_time_ms:50, wall_time_ms:50}) with a controlled tableReadDelayMs:200 and asserts /wall_time_ms budget exhausted/, so the overrun is forced by controlled host-call delay (200 vs 50) rather than by scheduler luck. My earlier claim came from a grep truncated by 'head -12' that showed only budget declarations - the same truncation error class as misreading the grep-filtered CI log. Consequence for the repair: the ONLY change needed is the shared happy-path default, raised from wall_time_ms 100 to 300000 (the canonical schema maximum, matching sibling worker-modes), which removes the machine-speed race from every ordinary invocation in the file while the deterministic exhaustion proof is untouched. Verified: no assertion pins the old shared 100 (the admission-boundary test supplies its own complete budget sets), and the file passes 16 assertions in 13537ms after the change.

Lane repair implemented as orthogonal first-class metadata rather than accumulated command-line exceptions. New test-resource-classification{,-constants}.js + generate-test-resource-classes.js mirror the primary classifier's fail-closed contract (unknown class, duplicate shard claim, shard naming a non-census path, census file missing from manifest, digest drift all hard-error; verified by injecting a bogus shard path). Classes ordinary/cpu-heavy/external-toolchain/exclusive with RESOURCE_CLASS_JOBS mapping external-toolchain->1. Membership is MEASURED: 14 entries carry their real/user/cores numbers, and two grep-matching files were excluded on evidence (node-shutdown-cell-worker-teardown 0.94s user, js-request-binding-example 0.85s user, versus 12.64s for the smallest genuine entry). Root cause of the leak also fixed one level up: generate-test-shards.js discovered integration files by walking test/integration, so it now asks derivePrimaryClasses instead - integration lanes went 59->73 files and all 14 leaked tests gained a serial home. test:fast now selects via scripts/plan-test-lane.js by class instead of a path glob. Contract tests that pinned the old shape were UPDATED, not weakened: project-hardening-contracts now follows the delegation (each lane must invoke run-test-files.js and must not use xargs -r, which silently runs nothing on empty input) and run-test-ci-overlapped now asserts ordinary keeps --jobs=4 and toolchain is --jobs=1.

MAJOR CORRECTION, and a systemic harness defect. I earlier claimed the wasm/service-cell tests 'declare no timeout'. False: they declare named constants, and the harness could not see them. run-test-files.js matched only /\{[^{}]*\btimeout:\s*(\d{4,})/ - literal digits - while system-guidelines forbids magic numbers, so the guideline-COMPLIANT declaration form was inert. My own grep reproduced the harness's blind spot, which is why I mis-reported it. Scope: 18 test files declared 45s-300s and every one silently ran under tap's bare 30s cap, including service-init-wasm-scaffold (300s declared via TOOLCHAIN_TIMEOUT_MS), service-cell-world-abi, service-cell-v2-world-abi, service-compiler-module-shape-spike, service-compiler-editor-typings, handler-aware-runtime-invocation and service-compiler-account-summary-parity (120s each), plus 10 integration/bootstrap files. This is the same class as the 2026-08-04 discovery recorded in that file (ten files with inert 45s-360s options); that repair handled literals and left named constants broken. Fixed by resolving same-file  declarations. Proof: service-init-wasm-scaffold failed at 36911ms at jobs=1 on two pinned cores with 'not ok 1 - timeout!', subtests 3 and 4 sharing an identical 35613.627ms, and the wizer 'failed to open directory' cascade - reproducing the hosted failure exactly - then passed at 37385ms once its own 300s declaration was honoured, with the wizer error gone and no change to wizer or the scaffold, confirming the cascade prediction.

Supplement to the inert-declaration finding, restoring a clause my shell mangled. The harness repair in run-test-files.js resolves same-file numeric const declarations of the form: const IDENTIFIER = 300000; (digit separators such as 300_000 allowed). TIMEOUT_OPTION_PATTERN now accepts either an identifier or digits after timeout:, and numericConstants() builds the identifier-to-value map from the same source file, so a declaration written as {timeout: TOOLCHAIN_TIMEOUT_MS} resolves to 300000ms and lifts TAP_TIMEOUT to 300s. Verified: the resolver returns 300000 for service-init-wasm-scaffold, eslint is clean, and 18 files change their effective TAP_TIMEOUT from the silent 30s cap to their authors declared 45s-300s. Loosening those 18 watchdogs is honouring an explicit author declaration rather than inventing headroom, and the per-file process kill (--timeout-ms, default 600s) still bounds every file regardless.

hypothesis: Resource-aware lane repair plus the harness timeout-contract fix. Added orthogonal resource classification (ordinary/cpu-heavy/external-toolchain/exclusive) with a fail-closed census and jobs=1 for external-toolchain; fixed the shard generator to discover by primary class rather than directory, re-homing 14 leaked integration-classified files (integration lanes 59 to 73); test:fast now selects by class via plan-test-lane.js; replaced regex timeout extraction with an espree-parsed fail-loud module resolving named constants, folded arithmetic and one-level imports, un-inerting 18 files that declared 45s-300s and silently ran at 30s; raised the shared happy-path wall_time_ms fixture off scheduler noise while leaving its controlled-delay exhaustion proof untouched; instrumented impact-proof-cone-consumers without retries.

claim: Independent subagent verification completed (evidence subagent:a7be5626e29bee23d). It CONFIRMED three claims with independent evidence: no correctness test weakened (every removed line re-added with only an added options argument; the deterministic wall-exhaustion proof at minimal-deployment-request-cell-runtime-readiness.test.js:546-565 verified intact, 200ms controlled delay against a 50ms budget = 4x margin, strictly stronger than the 100ms shared budget it replaced); the 18-file inert-declaration count exact (it recomputed 22 files now lifting, minus 4 newly declared = 18 pre-existing); and the resource classification measurement-based (it re-measured and reproduced the recorded numbers, and found no heavy toolchain test missing). It REFUTED the coverage claim and found a severe defect I introduced: moving the 14 leaked integration-classified files into the shard lanes removed them from every gate that runs, because the postpush manifest executes only test:fast and the shard lanes are reachable only from release.yml on a v* tag - so part of a green hosted gate would have come from 14 tests silently not running. My census test could not catch it because it asserted files are CLAIMED by a lane, never that a gate EXECUTES that lane.

Defects from independent verification, all repaired. (1) SEVERE, coverage: added test:fast:integration lane (primary=integration, --exclude-prefix test/integration/,test/bootstrap/, jobs=1) so the 14 files run on every push again, exactly as the old glob ran them, now serially instead of at jobs=4. Added a regression guard that reconstructs the OLD glob selection and asserts the push gate still runs all of it, plus a binding test asserting package.json's test:fast chain really invokes each modelled lane at the job count its resource class declares - negative-controlled by removing the lane from the chain and confirming the guard fails. (2) exact-election-evidence-same-turn-model-contract.test.js had been getting 60s only because the OLD regex matched a spawnSync timeout that is not a test declaration; the stricter parser correctly rejected it, silently regressing the file to 30s. Given an explicit {timeout: FILE_TIMEOUT_MS} on its test call (120000). (3) Extractor hardened against every silent-wrong input found: let/var bindings and any later assignment now mark a name ambiguous rather than resolving a stale literal; computed keys and spread-built options objects are reported; divide-by-zero and non-finite folds are reported instead of returning null; test.only/skip/todo now recognised. Five regression tests added (18 total). Re-scan: 2058 files, 0 problems. (4) censusDiagnosis made lazy - it was running a third full census walk on every green run because assert message arguments evaluate eagerly. (5) RESOURCE_CLASS_JOBS was decorative; now bound to the real lane commands by the binding test. (6) audit:shards now also checks the resource manifest. (7) Removed two stale exclude entries naming files that no longer exist.
